The Lincoln Memorial, a monumental tribute to Abraham Lincoln completed in nineteen twenty-two on the National Mall in Washington, D.C.

Designed by architect Henry Bacon in the Beaux-Arts style, modeled after the Parthenon, the memorial projects eternal grandeur and democratic ideals. The memorial's classical Doric temple design evokes timeless authority, and its symbolic placement anchoring the west end of the Mall made it the natural stage for momentous gatherings.

The sculpture was created by Daniel Chester French, one of America's greatest sculptors. The seated Lincoln figure, carved from Georgia marble and towering nineteen feet tall, depicts him in contemplation, hands resting on the chair's arms—a pose suggesting both strength and thoughtfulness. The massive bronze statue weighs one hundred seventy-five tons. It has become the visual symbol of Lincoln's legacy and American ideals of emancipation and democracy.

The memorial was constructed of Georgia white marble, Tennessee pink marble, and Colorado Yule marble—materials chosen for their durability and symbolic purity. Located at the western terminus of the National Mall, directly across from the Capitol, the memorial creates a symbolic dialogue about Lincoln's place in American history.

The interior walls inscribe Lincoln's Gettysburg Address and his Second Inaugural Address, framing the figure with his own words on union and freedom. The memorial became the site of Martin Luther King Junior's "I Have a Dream" speech in nineteen sixty-three, forever linking the memorial to the Civil Rights Movement and visions of equality. That moment remains one of history's most momentous orations, and it irrevocably shaped the memorial's significance for generations to come.
